old_title: South Africa v Australia: third men's cricket Test, day four - live
new_title: South Africa all out and set Australia 288 to win decider: third men's cricket Test, day four - as it happened
old_text:
95th over: South Africa 269-5 (Rickelton 74, Mulder 30) Cummins has a leg slip in place for Rickelton, who ignores the balls outside leg stump - one of which yields two byes - and defends the straight ones. This pair have been together for almost 30 overs now.
"Hello Rob," writes Gervase Greene. "There's been plenty of attention on Marnus Labuschagne's precarious position, but I think Nathan Lyon's future is almost as shaky.
"After a poor first Test, and being dropped for the second, his bowling has so far been patchy at best. Throughout his career he's been (sometimes harshly) judged for not wrapping up enough fourth innings... but this wicket is doing more than enough to justify a nation's expectations.
"And boy will he be aware of that."
I didn't realise he was quite so old - he turns 39 next month. I guess he's desperate to do the last lap and win in South Africa and/or India and/or England, but maybe it'll be taken out of his hands.
94th over: South Africa 267-5 (Rickelton 74, Mulder 30) Matt Renshaw replaces Lyon and has an appeal for a bat-pad catch turned down. The ball gripped and missed both inside edge and glove. A good over from Renshaw, another maiden.
"Why is Renshaw getting a twirl please?" asks Eamonn Maloney. "Not because he should be behind Head in the part-time pecking order but because we've got a second spinner, an all-rounder picked ostensibly in part for his bowling... or is he a part-timer too? If so, he should be picked on the strength of his batting and be in the top six?? He's bowled three of the 94."
It's a very English selection, though we usually do it in South Asia rather than South Africa.
92nd over: South Africa 267-5 (Rickelton 74, Mulder 30) A rare full ball from Lyon is scrunched down the ground for four by Rickelton. Lovely shot. He's playing seriously well.
"Clouds gathering ominously overhead, barely a breath of wind to blow them away," says Duncan Bonnett. "Luckily, I'm in Joburg, so no chance of it affecting the cricket. So, here's the deal: if we're still batting at tea, it'll be a great comeback and put the match back in the balance, although still pretty much in Australia's favour.
"If we can bat for an hour after tea, with some lusty swinging from Jansen et al, it's pretty even. However, one big partnership from the Aussies, and it's all over. So, we need to bat until halfway through the evening session, then get at least three wickets, maybe four before the close. Not gonna happen, is it?"
91st over: South Africa 261-5 (Rickelton 69, Mulder 29) Mulder squirts Cummins through point for a couple. Cummins decides to go to the short-ball ploy, which has worked so well in this series. Mulder takes it on and gets a single to long leg. South Africa lead by 161.
"That blitskrieg by Starc on day one is probably undervalued," writes George van Zijl. "Add another 50 runs for SA to this total and we have a big game on, perhaps even advantage SA."
90th over: South Africa 257-5 (Rickelton 68, Mulder 26) A maiden from Lyon to Mulder, who is playing a vital hand at No7. He has 26 from 67 balls, Rickelton a very neat 68 from 136.
"A lot of talk that 200 will be a lot to chase but is the wicket really that tricky?" asks Graeme Burton. "Lyon is bowling well without breaking through and the seamers are not looking particularly threatening. 200+ is tough in the fourth dig no matter the pitch but I dont think SA are that far ahead yet. What do you think?"
My instinct is that anything over 200 will be tricky, though I'm basing that more on historical precedent than this particular pitch.
Thanks Geoff, hello everyone. After two ultimately one-sided games, the series decider has developed into the most compelling arm-wrestle. Ryan Rickelton has a highest Test score of 259, against Pakistan last year, but in context this could become his best innings.
89th over: South Africa 257-5 (Rickelton 68, Mulder 26) The Rickelton cover drive again! This one more conventional. Cummins the bowler, but it doesn't matter. Cummins pulls the length back a notch, puts everything into finding some seam movement, and there is just a touch. A scintilla. An iota. But the work required to get it is notable. Rickelton is beaten by one that goes away, then leaves one that nibbles back. Tight line to the off stump, length not full enough to hit it though, and Rickelton is this confident now.
With that, it is time for the drinks break, and with the drinks break, it is time for Rob Smyth, rubbing his little hands together with glee like a raccoon about to dive into a bin.
88th over: South Africa 252-5 (Rickelton 64, Mulder 25) Not much in the way of attack against Rickelton now. Most of the catchers have been sent to sun in the fields of their youth. Only short leg remains. Around, the lone and level sands stretch far away.
87th over: South Africa 252-5 (Rickelton 64, Mulder 25) This is creeping into Advantage South Africa territory. Even if a wicket falls now, a Jansen flurry can take their lead from 150 past 200, and 200 will take some getting. Rickelton shows his growing confidence with a handsome cover drive from Starc, not an overpitched ball but on the up. There's been very little lateral movement from this pitch all match.
86th over: South Africa 246-5 (Rickelton 59, Mulder 24) Lyon gets the new ball now, with the hope that it will give him more bounce. He is a bounce bowler. He's bowling well, too, lots of loop and drop. Gets one that jumps at Mulder, beats the edge, hits the pad, loops up to leg slip. There's no one there, and no touch on the ball, but the batter had little idea what was happening.
85th over: South Africa 244-5 (Rickelton 58, Mulder 24) Has to react quickly to Starc's bounce and pace, but Rickelton is able to deflect his cut shot behind point for two, then gloves a ball down for a run to the leg side. I wouldn't fancy wearing Starc's pace on the gloves. That hurt Rickelton too, he's shaking his fingers at the other end with the glove off.
84th over: South Africa 241-5 (Rickelton 55, Mulder 24) He's building here! Ryan Rickelton is saying, I have the discipline today but I have the shots as well. Produces another of those, driving Hazlewood gloriously through wide long off.
83rd over: South Africa 236-5 (Rickelton 50, Mulder 24) Jaffa from Starc! Line tight to the off stump, hard length that rises at Mulder, and the seam movement takes the ball away. Mulder lucky to be beaten. Then lucky to get four. Another drive, a big edge and the new ball flies away through the gap.
82nd over: South Africa 232-5 (Rickelton 50, Mulder 20) Hazlewood the other new-ball operator, and Rickelton soon finds a single, raising his fifty. He's played so well. Got monstered in Durban, didn't make a significant contribution in Gqeberha, but he's played an essential hand here. More needed, but a lead of 132 already gives them something to work with.
What's with the field, though? Rickelton has hardly been slashing a lot of balls from outside off stump to the fence. He has, however, collected singles wherever possible. So why have a deep point, giving him one?
81st over: South Africa 230-5 (Rickelton 49, Mulder 19) The shiny varnished Kooka flies out of the box. You don't imagine you'll see anything like Starc produced on evening one, because that was in cloudy conditions late in the day, and right now it's sunny with a breeze across the ground, but one never knows. The umpire has held onto the new ball for now, Starc begins the 81st over with the old one. Sends down one loosener, then asks Ump Illy for the new one. But wastes it first up, on the hip and glanced for four. Was looking for swing into the right handed Mulder, but started too straight and too short. Now goes across him. Then has Mulder driving in the air! But it doesn't go to hand, it goes for three.
80th over: South Africa 222-5 (Rickelton 48, Mulder 16) Last one before the newy, and Rick-Ry takes the single early in his preferred style. Mulder attacks again, seeing width outside off, and a very wristy square drive, a Kohli style hockey snap of the wrists, but where Kohli usually uses that movement to play the ball through long on, Mulder turns his wrists around so that goes in a different direction by 90 degrees, through cover point. Some shot.
79th over: South Africa 216-5 (Rickelton 47, Mulder 11) The Patented Rickelton Strike Rotator is into effect again, cutting Lyon behind point. At which stage, Mulder says, singles be damned. Smotes Lyon for six! Full enough for the shot, and Mulder picks it up with a lofted on-drive over wide long on. Lyon changes to bowling around the wicket for the right-hander, and immediately has him in jeopardy to the ball straightening down the line of the stumps, Mulder made to work hard to keep a couple out.
78th over: South Africa 209-5 (Rickelton 46, Mulder 5) Renshaw with another, and reward for Rickelton's patience as he gets a shorter one that sits up nicely enough to be whipped away through square leg. Four runs, and a single to follow, he has kept the singles coming even if Mulder has not yet.
77th over: South Africa 204-5 (Rickelton 41, Mulder 5) One run from Lyon's over. They're both playing him off the back foot a lot, and he looks like he's in the game when that happens, pads right in front of stumps, catchers waiting. Just the one wicket for Lyon so far this innings, he needs to deliver on this sense of menace.
76th over: South Africa 203-5 (Rickelton 40, Mulder 5) Don't get out in the over before lunch? Tick. Don't get out in the over after lunch? Tick. Call him Ryan Tickelton. Defending stoutly. It might seem incongruous to have Renshaw as the post-prandial bowler, but he's ticking off a last couple of overs before the second new ball.
Lunch - South Africa 202 for 5, lead by 102 in the third innings
They're still in it. An even session, only 62 runs added, but it would have been huge for SA had Breetzke still been there. Still, they've got their lead past 100, and if they can double that then they'll be a real show to win this Test. A partnership between these two, some big swings from Big Marco, and that 200 lead could be theirs.
75th over: South Africa 202-5 (Rickelton 39, Mulder 5) Starc for a second over, annoyed with an extra walk-back and run-up as Mulder pulls out. And if he was annoyed the first time, imagine the second time. Consecutive balls. Starc can't blame the batter too much though, because the second time was about the towel falling out of the bowler's waistband. Nasty bouncer, once he's finally allowed to bowl. Mulder glides the next away, wants a single but Rickelton ignores him, and Mulder isn't impressed. Might be in the hangry zone with lunch looming. So is Starc, who gets stuck into Mulder about running on the pitch. It's a preoccupation of Starc's in recent times, with a few batters, he gets stroppy about that.
It doesn't get him a wicket though. One no-ball in the over, and that is that.
74th over: South Africa 201-5 (Rickelton 39, Mulder 5) Australia think they have Rickelton's wicket! Absolutely convinced. But they're wrong. Renshaw is the bowler, spinner. There's a huge puff of dust from the ball pitching outside the off stump, and that dust is stirred up again as the toe of the bat clips the ground, I think, or just whooshes through that dust cloud. The ball ends up at slip, but the deflection was not from the outside edge of the bat. Big Rick survives. Big Ren bowls a maiden.
73rd over: South Africa 201-5 (Rickelton 39, Mulder 5) Starc back for Cummins, which is interesting, as he'll be the new-ball operator, surely. Maybe just two overs here, for something different, then a quick break? Rickelton flashes him away to deep third. Mulder drives at him and nearly edges. That's the left-arm angle to a right-hander.
72nd over: South Africa 200-5 (Rickelton 38, Mulder 5) They're a hundred to the good! A single from Lyon completes that. An appeal against Mulder as he pads the ball away, but manages to keep the gloves clear.
71st over: South Africa 199-5 (Rickelton 37, Mulder 5) Rickelton is playing Cummins to the leg side really well, the bowler over the wicket to the lefty, and a bit too full, allowing the batter to go back down the ground again.
70th over: South Africa 194-5 (Rickelton 32, Mulder 5) Lyon is ragging it. Every time he hits that rough patch outside off stump, it turns big. Back in and nearly bowls Mulder, hits Carey again and bounces away, Mulder had no idea where that ball was going. Threatening for South Africa now, but it increases the urgency with which the Australians need to get through this innings. Harmer will have plenty to work with in defending a target. The lead is 94.
69th over: South Africa 194-5 (Rickelton 32, Mulder 5) Comical misfield from Green, as Rickelton punches through point. He's chasing, he slides, and then the slide just stops. Holds up in the grass. He throws out one huge arm to try to grab the ball just inside the rope, but his fingertips can't drag it in. Cummins concedes four.
68th over: South Africa 189-5 (Rickelton 28, Mulder 4) Four catchers around the bat for Mulder, though he turns things over well enough. Rickelton ups the ante to end the over, a full ball at leg stump that he drives very nicely, straight, just to the on side of straight, for four.
WICKET! Breetzke c Starc b Cummins 43, South Africa 181-5
Matthew Breetzke, what have you done? Straight to your room without dinner. That is... so predictable. So easy. So unnecessary. Cummins with an old ball, he will eventually go short, and it seems that Breetzke is waiting for that. Because on this pitch with the old ball, it doesn't get up that high. He's waiting for the pull shot but only takes it from about waist height, can't get power on it, can't get elevation on it, can't keep it down either. Hits it off his hip in the air, a nice flat curve to long leg, where Starc takes the catch. After 372 balls without one, Cummins finally takes a wicket. That will have given his career strike rate a beating.
66th over: South Africa 181-4 (Breetzke 43, Rickelton 24) There he goes! Breetzke plays the shot that Bavuma played last night, except that he hits it. The result is four to the midwicket boundary, a standing slog sweep across the line. Then a single to raise the fifty stand. They're batted really well, done some hard work, and have room to make the most of that for a while until the second new ball creates new challenges. Almost a strange dismissal for Rickelton though! Pads the ball away from outside leg, but holds his bat up at shoulder height, and the ball comes up and hits that bat. Luckily for him the rebound drops safely towards point, not to a fielder.
65th over: South Africa 176-4 (Breetzke 39, Rickelton 24) Cummins to the right-hander. Two slips, quite staggered. And finally the scoring dam lets through a little water. Overpitched a touch, and Breetzke drives through extra cover for four. Drives again, straighter now, so Cummins gets fingertips to it and deflects it to mid off, no run.
64th over: South Africa 171-4 (Breetzke 34, Rickelton 24) Lyon now over the wicket to Rickelton, who is kicking away everything he can that pitches outside his leg stump, as a left-hander. The grind continues.
63rd over: South Africa 171-4 (Breetzke 34, Rickelton 24) Pat Cummins to give things a go after the break, and his surprise ball is that he doesn't bowl a bouncer. Not one. Not in a whole over. Is he feeling alright? He's enduring his longest wicketless stretch in his career, since last taking one in Durban, though he bowled excellently yesterday.
62nd over: South Africa 171-4 (Breetzke 34, Rickelton 24) Edged and hits the keeper! Not a chance, really, hits Carey on the pad too low to catch, off the inside edge as Breetzke comes forward. The ricochet doesn't go to hand, even with all those catchers grouped around. A drinks break arrives, for all to recompose themselves.
61st over: South Africa 170-4 (Breetzke 33, Rickelton 24) I lied about the quicks bowling half these overs, because Cooper Connolly will bowl at least one of them. Might only be one, as he starts with a drag-down that Breetzke cuts through cover for four. Connolly is a left-arm ortho with a first-class bowling record that barely exists, yet is discussed in Test terms as an all-rounder. One of life's great mysteries. Five singles later, and his over has gone for nine.
60th over: South Africa 161-4 (Breetzke 26, Rickelton 22) Not an easy over for Rickelton to face, a maiden from Lyon. Edges one ball into his leg, misses another while stepping across and trying to whip to the leg side, hopping about on one leg and nearly falling over trying to keep it out of his pads.
59th over: South Africa 161-4 (Breetzke 26, Rickelton 22) Another tidy over from Hazlewood, not creating any threat though as yet. Goes the short ball a couple of times, that is probably method number one for the Australian quicks right now, with 21 overs to go until the new ball. Lyon will bowl half of those, so it's up to the fast men to find some way of applying pressure with the rest.
58th over: South Africa 159-4 (Breetzke 25, Rickelton 21) Huge shout for Lyon against Breetzke, hit him outside the line but he had his bat tucked behind pad. Not sure if the umpire said he was playing a shot or no. Australia only have one review left, so they don't chance it on whether that Lyon ball was turning back enough. I say no, at a glance.
57th over: South Africa 158-4 (Breetzke 24, Rickelton 21) I'm really enjoying seeing the South Africans fight out some good overs, and leave scoring to later. Hazlewood to Rickelton, had his number in Durban when Rickelton was opening, but he's now the keeper in the middle order, and he's determined not to make a mistake. Defends the entire over with laser focus.
56th over: South Africa 158-4 (Breetzke 24, Rickelton 21) Lyon with four fielders in a star formation around the right-handed Breetzke, and you sense that Lyon is where the persistent menace will be. Big turn, and a few little yelps and murmurs from the fielders as Breetzke isn't far from popping one up.
55th over: South Africa 157-4 (Breetzke 24, Rickelton 20) Hazlewood on for a jam roll. Rickelton doesn't play him badly, tries to go as gently at the ball as possible, so when an edge is found, it rolls away for a couple of runs. The South African have been good this morning, haven't tried to force the pace like their top order did yesterday to the team's detriment.
54th over: South Africa 154-4 (Breetzke 24, Rickelton 17) The left-hander keeps chopping Lyon behind point, a run there, then Breetzke plays tip-and-run to mid on. Umpire Illingworth scolds him for running down the middle of the pitch, but it was a tight one, he might have been out had be detoured to the side. Not that you're allowed to traipse up and down the centre of the strip all day, even with that excuse. You get leeway on one of those, then probably a warning on the next.
Match calculations here are easy: South Africa's lead is their score minus 100. They lead by 54.
53rd over: South Africa 151-4 (Breetzke 23, Rickelton 15) Starc goes around the wicket to Breetzke, and is going at him. The batter is getting drawn into the conflict, a bit of lip flying back and forth. Starc is bowling rapidly, and that angle into the right hander can be difficult. Breetzke negotiates the over, defending and ducking where he can, but Starc looks dangerous. No runs.
52nd over: South Africa 151-4 (Breetzke 23, Rickelton 15) There they go! Rickelton gets a ball from Lyon that is not exactly short, but the batter gets back and leans away to make the length and the width he wants, cuts behind point for four. One good partnership and this could very much be South Africa's day.
"Morning Geoff. Fire up the CRUCIAL FIRST SESSION machine, this really will decide the match. I'm wondering, do you think South Africa missed a trick with only one frontline spinner here? Given the turn and it only getting more exaggerated through the game, Lyon is backed up by Connolly and Renshaw? Coetzee hasn't really fired - yet - so you wonder what Maharaj could've done here..."
Morning, Guy Hornsby. I think they got burned by two spinners at Durban and were never going to return to it here. But with enough runs, Harmer should be able to do most of the job alone, and Markram can support if necessary.
51st over: South Africa 147-4 (Breetzke 23, Rickelton 11) Starc off his long, long run, turning on the advertising cloths that are pegged to the turf. Length ball, bouncer, then Rickelton gets a thick outside edge to deep point and is able to take a run. Breetzke carries on defending from the crease, then hops about, thinks about picking up the ball. Don't do it, Matthew. There's a fair bit of chat going on out there too, Starc with that broad smile he uses when he's needling somebody. He's quite an innocuous chat merchant usually, doesn't have that particular dog in him.
50th over: South Africa 146-4 (Breetzke 23, Rickelton 10) Breetzke has to dive into his ground going through for a single, after getting in a tangle with Lyon as the batter set off from the non-striker's end. That could have been an interesting one, had the throw hit the stumps. Probably home. Rickelton gets that run, Breetzke adds a couple more, but the top-edged sweep is not a sustainable method against this bowler.
49th over: South Africa 143-4 (Breetzke 21, Rickelton 9) Lyon and Starc will be the opening combo. Starc took 6-72 in the first innings, and has 2-29 so far this time around. He only had a couple of 10-wicket matches in a long career until recently, then added two more within the past 12 months. Another one is in the frame if he's good enough.
Breetzke scrambles a semblance of a shot against a short ball, deflecting a single from a tangle of gloves. Rickelton plays with more elan, steering to backward point in the deep.
48th over: South Africa 141-4 (Breetzke 20, Rickelton 8) It will be Nathan Lyon to start things off, from the end where he knocked over Bavuma in the second-last over last night. Early single to Breetzke, and Lyon comes around the wicket to the left-handed Rickelton, with three catchers on the off side! You don't often see that. Two slips and a silly mid-off. Defensively played.
And what of yesterday? It was another belter, shifting back and forth, but so much rests on South Africa's captain, and while he was there, the hosts were in the best spot. Until the very late hour, the day's final passage of play... here's the match report.
If Temba Bavuma was decisive for South Africa as he batted through day after day in Gqeberha, his fall in the shadow of stumps on the third day might prove as decisive at Cape Town. Bowled by a Nathan Lyon classic with eight balls to go, he saw his team reach stumps at 140 for 4, with a lead of just 40 to build on.
Hello, sport fiends. It is your season. Once again, as has been our good fortune through this Test match, we approach a new day of it with intrigue in the air and with any option possible. South Africa will resume their third innings four wickets down with a lead of just 40. In the next session, so much will be decided. Wickets, and Australia press home their advantage and set themselves up for a manageable chase. But it won't take too many runs to become a big problem for the visitors. Another hundred and the game is alive, and two hundred and the game is snarling and destroying its cage.
Because it ain't the easiest to bat out there, the pitch is wearing and offering more turn to the spinners, while still some lift for the quicks, even though batters can still play shots on it with true bounce. It might be a surface that rewards judicious aggression today, and South Africa have Breetzke, Rickleton, Mulder, Jansen, and Harmer to come, who can all meet that brief.
The whole series is genuinely in the balance as of ball one.
new_text:
It would be unfair to say that Australia let a winning position slip on the fourth day of the third Test at Cape Town, only because that would undersell how Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder prised it away.
Australia's vaunted four bowlers, owners of 1,674 wickets at day's beginning, could only raise that to 1678 by day's end. In the process, a lead of 40 became 287. South Africa had been 40 for 4 in the first innings at Gqeberha and bounced back to win; they were effectively 40 for 4 in the third innings here, and now have a great chance to do the same.
South Africa were in danger of losing the series today. Instead, Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder made superb, methodical centuries to take them to 387 all out. I still have no idea who are the favourites, but we should get a positive result one way or the other.
Thanks for your company and emails, and sorry again for my addled state. Geoff's report will be here shortly, and he'll be back for the start of day five. It could be a classic.
134th over: South Africa 387-9 (Mulder 115, Rabada 2) Make that four sixes for Mulder, who has just dumped Lyon over the leg side and into the crowd. Time for one more over. When they resumed on 140 for 4, South Africa couldn't have imagined they would still be batting at the close.
133rd over: South Africa 380-9 (Mulder 108, Rabada 2) A length ball from Cummins is boffed over backward square leg for six by Mulder. That's a helluva shot, his third six of the innings, and he keeps the strike with a single off the fifth delivery.
132nd over: South Africa 372-9 (Mulder 101, Rabada 2) Mulder drives Lyon through extra cover for two to reach a fantastic hundred! It's his fourth in Tests - and arguably his best yet even though he has a highest score of 367 not out.
Mulder came in with South Africa effectively 81 for 5, knowing the series would be over if he fell early. But he played serenely from the start, always looked in control and reached his century from 204 balls.
131st over: South Africa 369-9 (Mulder 98, Rabada 2) Mulder again takes a single off the fourth ball of the over, and Rabada takes care of business without alarm.
Some of the commentators think South Africa should declare, which makes no sense when their lead is only 269.
"Cordially disagree with Roland Marshall," begins Phil Harrison. "270 is a really tough chase for anyone, let alone a team who have been batting like Australia have and who are missing their best player. A Travis Head special changes things obviously, but to me, this feels like SA's to lose now. What a game though. Nothing like Test cricket is there?"
It's the best thing that has ever happened to anyone, ever.
130th over: South Africa 368-9 (Mulder 97, Rabada 2) Mulder again takes a single off the fourth ball, this time with Lyon the bowler, and Rabada does the necessary thereafter.
"Afternoon Rob," writes Eddy Nason. "Fascinated that you went for Neil Finn when Catatonia (Mulder and Scully) were right there... was it an Homage to Neil's long lost brother Steve?"
My brain is not the most sophisticated organ - it's literally because, for no particular reason, I've had that Neil Finn song on loop the last few days. (But while we're here, Steven Finn is one of my favourite punduits and you should all read his book.)
129th over: South Africa 367-9 (Mulder 96, Rabada 2) Cummins, on for Starc, is pulled expertly for four by Mulder. Another pull for a single takes him to 96 and leaves Rabada with two balls to survive.
"Hi Rob," writes Roland Marshall. "Though there's a lot of cricket still to be played, the cheap wickets of Jansen and Harmer have the feeling of being more than pivotal here: both could have taken the game away from the Aussies with a sufficiently controlled bit of humpty. One would think that Australia are now in the ascendancy, especially with the prospect of Travis Head doing one of his fourth-innings yahoos.
"By the way, all the best with toiling through the OBO stricken; I did something similar about fifteen years ago, translating the live feed in real-time for a sporting event, with the flu. Because I was working on the back office of the event's IT system and every update came with a helpful 'ting!' I was able to do micro-naps between each entry. Bit more difficult for your good self, what with having to keep your eyes open and watch stuff."
Ah, thank you. Even when I'm sick as a dog, and I most certainly am, I know how lucky I am to do this job!
128th over: South Africa 362-9 (Mulder 91, Rabada 2) Mulder slog-sweeps Lyon for six to move into the nineties. Yeeeeeehaaaaaaaa!
This has been an innings of admirable substance. I must confess, from afar I thought Mulder was a bits-and-pieces player but he has proved me wrong in this series with bat and ball
127th over: South Africa 355-9 (Mulder 84, Rabada 2) Mulder turns down a single, then pulls Starc round the corner for one. I think he thought it was going for two or even four.
Starc knocks himself off his feet, Mark Wood-style, before being chipped for two by Rabada. There are certainly worse No11s in world cricket.
"I won't often get the chance for a pun to fit this snugly," begins Mike Morris. "So: poor old Rickelton fell victim to a case of Mulder and scurry.
"And with that I'm taking the rest of the day off."
Apparently a message was brought out from the South African dressing-room between overs, presumably because they want to bowl tonight. That feels like a pretty big risk when the lead is only 250.
But it's on the cards now, because Coetzee has been run out. He tried to take an imaginary single to short third, was sent back by Mulder and beaten by a direct hit from Labuschagne. Outstanding work from Labuschagne.
125th over: South Africa 347-8 (Mulder 78, Coetzee 1) Starc is one away from his fifth ten-for in Tests. He almost gets it when Coetzee gloves a unpleasant delivery over the head of Head at short leg. South Africa lead by 247.
124th over: South Africa 346-8 (Mulder 77, Coetzee 1) "Albert Edward Trott was the man who hit the six," says Tom Barrington. "Sure this will be a footnote in the carnage unfolding though!"
Harmer pads up to a classic off-break from Lyon that turns a long way to hit the off stump. Australia have taken three wickets for nine runs, South Africa lead by 244 and there is not a person on the planet who truly knows which team is on top.
123rd over: South Africa 344-7 (Mulder 76, Harmer 1) That was Starc's ninth wicket of the match. He's the dictionary definition of a champion fast bowler.
"I don't remember who it was, but didn't an English batsman once play at Lord's with a bout of malaria?" asks Anthony Bradley. "Came in before lunch on the first day, could barely see the ball, so decided to hit through the line and hit a six over the pavilion. It being Lord's, no-one applauded for the rash shot. When I'm awake at 4am, one thought distracts me more than any other: had England picked Jimmy Anderson and Ollie Robinson last winter, they might have won the Ashes.

"I think Stephen Fleming could be an excellent foil to many of this England Test team," writes Guy Hornsby. "I still find so much of the opprobrium towards Brook baffling as time goes on. I just cut and paste the emails. But yes, I agree, Test cricket is the purest form of sport in the whole wide world. Imagine if this was a five-Test series!

If you exclude the 1980s West Indies on the grounds of balance, I guess Australia are the attack with the strongest weak link. Brett Lee was bloody good, terrifying at times, but ultimately he averaged over 30. Mind you, do does Nathan Lyon. I can see both sides!
(I think you underestimate Gillespie btw - at his best, from 1997 t0 2004, he was a monster.)
The players are wandering back onto the field. By the way, I should apologise for the relative poverty of today's coverage - I'm sick as a dog (weirdly, this being the year 2026, I think I have Covid for the first time) but am soldiering on like an ersatz Gary Cooper.

100th over: South Africa 288-5 (Rickelton 80, Mulder 43) Cummins continues to roll the dice, brings Travis Head into the attack. Four singles form a low-key over.

"There have been a few Rourke's Drift performances to be fair, but chances are we'd be seeing Brook flattering to deceive, holing out for 30-odd. How deeply has Bazball penetrated English cricket's DNA, despite the encouraging cameos of 'proper batting' of late.
"As for Starc (you saw what I did there)....a large part of resilience is the ability to attack, to make it easier for those doing the hard graft to be, well, resilient."
I still think history will be kind to Bazball, however shambolically it ended. But it'll be fascinating to see them adopt a more streetwise approach under Stephen Fleming.
